annotations.keyFindings: Complete-entry days 91 percent with the electronic diary against 64 percent with paper among 164 adults; paper often filled in just before appointments.
annotations.limitations: Did not examine treatment decisions or appointments; older participants preferred paper.

annotations.keyFindings: Of 620 appointments, 31 percent had no usable diary; the eligibility decision was deferred in 58 percent of those, adding a median of 11 weeks.

claims.text: Among 620 specialist appointments, 31 percent of patients had no usable diary and the eligibility decision was deferred in 58 percent of them.
claims.passage: Among them, the eligibility decision was deferred to a further appointment in 58 percent.
claims.interpretation: Repeat appointments caused by missing diaries are a real cost to price.

claims.text: Appointments without a usable diary were 6 minutes longer on average.
claims.passage: Appointments without a usable diary were 6 minutes longer on average than appointments with one
claims.interpretation: Clinic time saved per complete diary can be costed.

claims.text: Nurse set-up of a symptom app took a median of 14 minutes per patient, and 22 percent needed a second session.
claims.passage: The median set-up time was 14 minutes per patient, and 22 percent of patients needed a second session.
claims.interpretation: Set-up time is the main new cost of the switch for the clinic.

claims.text: Better documentation was projected to raise the number of patients eligible for injectable preventives by 18 percent, at 4,900 per treated patient per year.
claims.passage: Better documentation of headache days was projected to raise the number of eligible patients by 18 percent
claims.interpretation: The largest financial consequence of the switch lies outside the clinic, in the drug budget.

claims.text: Electronic diaries had complete entries on 91 percent of days against 64 percent for paper.
claims.passage: Days with a complete entry were 91 percent with the electronic diary and 64 percent with paper.
claims.interpretation: The effectiveness question on completeness already has a randomised answer.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A randomised crossover study found electronic diaries far more complete than paper, so completeness has been compared already. Missing diaries lengthen appointments by about 6 minutes and defer eligibility decisions for injectable preventives in over half of affected patients, adding weeks and repeat appointments. App set-up costs nurse time, more for older patients, many of whom lack smartphones. Better documentation may raise the number of patients eligible for injectable preventives, so the largest financial consequence lies in the drug budget.
gradeRationale: One small randomised crossover study on completeness; the costing inputs are observational or model-based and from other settings.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five claims; overall certainty low.
